records.bodyText:
A sincere thank you to Hethersgill Parish Council and residents from across the surrounding communities for welcoming North Carlisle Against Pylons and Substation (NCAPS) to our latest community meeting.
The strength of feeling was unmistakable, with residents and farmers expressing deep concerns about National Grid's proposed Cross Border Connection, the extensive pylon route and the potential North Cumbria mega-substation at Option A.
The meeting brought several important outcomes:
 Growing political recognition: We welcomed David Allen, Labour's mayoral candidate, who made clear his view that Option A was the wrong location for the proposed substation — a statement met with applause. He also committed to working with affected communities and ensuring their concerns are heard should he become Mayor.
 Strengthening the campaign: We outlined the establishment of NCAPS Community Action Limited, providing a formal structure to raise funds, secure specialist legal and technical advice, and mount an evidence-led challenge to the pylon route, its design and the proposed substation location.
 Communities working together: Continued collaboration with the North Cumbria Parish Council Alliance will help ensure communities across the affected area have a coordinated and effective voice.
 Holding Cumberland Council to account: Our petition will be presented to Full Council on 3 November, calling on the Council to take a more proactive role in assessing the cumulative impacts of these proposals and representing affected communities.
It was also encouraging to reflect that representatives from across the mayoral political parties have now engaged with our communities, with concerns about the adequacy of National Grid's consultation extending across party lines.
We are not against upgrading the electricity network. We are challenging how and where that infrastructure is being proposed, and the potentially irreversible consequences for North Cumbria.
More than a year of uncertainty is already taking its toll on residents, farmers and businesses. Continued community engagement, fundraising and support will be essential as NCAPS moves into its next phase.
Thank you again to Hethersgill for hosting us and to everyone who attended, spoke openly and offered their support.
Our greatest strength remains the collective voice of our communities. We need to keep that momentum going.
#NCAPS #NorthCumbria #Hethersgill #CrossBorderConnection #NationalGrid #CommunityVoice #Carlisle

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
THE Scottish Government is facing questions over a minister’s letter which appeared to cast doubt on a commitment to introduce national planning guidance for huge, energyintensive data centres.
Public Finance Minister Hannah Mary Goodlad wrote to Scottish Green MSP Patrick Harvie on October 8 saying ministers were still considering whether to bring forward guidance for hyperscale developments.
However, the letter came just two days after Ms Goodlad confirmed in a written parliamentary answer that the guidance would be published before Christmas. She had also told MSPS in September that the government would bring forward national planning guidance by the end of the year.

records.bodyText:
Extraordinary!  
Following the Evershed and Ofgem reports on the state of NESO, the CEO of NESO, Fintan Slye, has been caught on a recording, stating that he knew about the issues - and did....nothing.  
This is known from a Times piece, below.  This is Kathryn Porter's take on it:
·
According to @thetimes @neso_energy CEO Fintan Slye who earned just under £1 million last year admitted he knew about the control room concerns but failed to act on them saying Neso may have incorrectly prioritised other things at a time when there was a “huge amount of change happening in the organisation”
How does the Times know this?
Because somebody inside NESO recorded the meeting and gave it to the press
Clearly NESO staff have lost confidence in their execs and have no issues embarrassing them in public
Although it's fair to ask why Fintan didn't make his mea culpa public himself. Perhaps he simply didn't want to admit either to getting it wrong or to allowing the focus on CP2030 and keeping the government happy to get in the way of keeping the grid secure 
There's a clear public interest in knowing this so I hope Fintan and NESO don't respond to this by trying to hunt the people who made and released this recording
The more productive approach would be to repair trust with staff, listen to and act on their concerns over grid security, and ensure cultural change so future concerns can be raised and acted on internally without staff feeling they have no options other than to leave or go to MPs and the media
https://www.thetimes.com/.../power-grid-boss-admits-he...
'The boss of the National Energy System Operator has admitted that he was aware of serious cultural issues at the government-owned body and failed to address them. 
Fintan Slye, who has been paid more than £770,000 a year to lead the organisation responsible for managing Britain’s power system, told staff he was “disappointed” in himself and “should have fixed” the problems before an independent report raised them. 
National Energy System Operator (Neso) is under scrutiny after whistleblowers raised concerns about its ability to keep the lights on and how it handled tight power supplies during the heatwave in June. 
An independent report published on Monday by Eversheds Sutherland, a law firm, could not substantiate specific whistleblower allegations that Neso deliberately altered operational records and took steps to avoid public scrutiny, or that corporate affairs personnel interfered in operational decisions in June.
However, Eversheds did find wider “control, cultural and governance issues”, which the energy regulator, Ofgem, described as “important and concerning” and which the government has told Neso to address “without delay”.
Eversheds highlighted four main underlying issues: “high levels of operational stress, a significant disconnect between the [control room] and executive leadership, a culture of reputational sensitivity affecting the perception of operational independence, and a gap between formal [whistleblowing] commitments and the lived experience of staff”.
In calls with Neso staff, recordings of which have been obtained by The Times, Slye admitted: “There’s nothing in any of those four themes that was a huge surprise, or that I could put my hand on my heart and say that I haven’t heard that from someone in the organisation.” Slye said the Eversheds report had made “difficult reading”.
“I’m disappointed in myself, in that we haven’t acted sooner to address [the issues], or more comprehensively to address them, such that they ended up having to be raised in a form and in a format like this,” he said. 
Asked by a staff member why the issues hadn’t been addressed, he suggested Neso may have incorrectly prioritised other things at a time when there was a “huge amount of change happening in the organisation”, but said he had no “easy answer” for why it had failed to act. “The answer is: I should have fixed them. I should have leant in to try, and got them fixed.”
He added: “All I can do is hold up my hands and say we will fix them now.”
Slye also admitted: “Sometimes I can be defensive, and I have to absolutely make sure that my reaction to this is not that.” 
A Neso spokesman said: “Slye’s comments referred to the broader organisational and cultural themes identified by the independent Eversheds Sutherland investigation, not the specific allegations, which the investigation did not substantiate. He was clear with colleagues that Neso should have acted sooner and more comprehensively on those wider themes, we accept that and are taking action to address them.” 
Slye received total pay, bonuses and other remuneration of £773,650 as chief executive of Neso in 2024-25, the last year for which accounts are available. He was separately paid a further £156,870 by National Grid that year under a performance scheme linked to the creation of the nationalised Neso. 
Michael Shanks, the energy minister, has said that the independent review “raises areas for cultural improvement in Neso where we expect significant action without delay”. 
Asked about Slye’s admission that he was already aware of the issues and failed to tackle them, a government source indicated that it retained full confidence in Slye.'

WHO IS LISTENING TO THE PEOPLE KEEPING BRITAIN’S LIGHTS ON?
An independent investigation has identified serious weaknesses in NESO’s culture and governance, including concerns about whether frontline engineers are being heard.
Emergency electricity assistance from Europe. Grid bottlenecks preventing power reaching consumers. Expensive interventions to keep the system balanced.
And Ofgem’s technical investigation into June’s grid events remains unfinished.
These are serious questions about the electricity system our homes, businesses and essential services depend upon.
Before ministers push Britain further towards dependence on electricity, they must demonstrate that the system can deliver—and explain the full cost to the people paying for it.
MAKE THEM SHOW THE EVIDENCE.
